experiments.name: Cylinder wake
experiments.question: How does the wake change with Reynolds number?

presets.label: Steady wake (Re 40)
presets.name: Steady Wake (Re 40)
presets.question: Below what Reynolds number does the wake stop shedding?
presets.blurb: The same cylinder at Re = 40. Viscosity damps the instability: the flow separates but the two recirculation bubbles behind the body stay attached and symmetric.

presets.label: Vortex shedding (Re 180)
presets.name: Kármán Vortex Street
presets.question: How does the wake change with Reynolds number?
presets.blurb: A circular cylinder in a steady stream at Re = 180. The wake is unstable and sheds a staggered train of counter-rotating vortices, and the transverse velocity at a wake probe oscillates at the shedding frequency.

compare.text: Steady versus shedding wake at the same size and speed (matched elapsed convective time).

experiments.name: Airfoil lift
experiments.question: How do geometry and angle affect circulation, separation and signed lift?

presets.name: Airfoil at −14°
presets.question: Is the lift antisymmetric in the angle of attack?
presets.blurb: The mirror image of the +14° scene. The suction side is now the lower surface and the lift coefficient should be negative with a similar magnitude.

presets.label: 0° baseline
presets.name: Airfoil at 0° (baseline)
presets.question: Does a symmetric airfoil at zero angle produce zero lift?
presets.blurb: The symmetric airfoil aligned with the flow. The wake is symmetric and thin; any lift measured is noise from the unsteady wake crossing the circulation contour.

presets.name: Airfoil at +14°
presets.question: How do geometry and angle affect circulation, separation and signed lift?
presets.blurb: A symmetric airfoil at a positive angle of attack. Flow accelerates over the upper surface, separates near the trailing edge, and the deflected wake carries the momentum of the lift.

compare.text: Zero-angle baseline versus +14°: circulation-derived lift appears; drag from the wake deficit is approximate.
Angle reversal at matched conditions: C_l changes sign with similar magnitude.

experiments.name: Cycling and drafting
experiments.question: How does a second rider change the wake and the drag estimate?

presets.label: Single rider
presets.name: Rider Silhouette
presets.question: How large is the wake behind a single rider?
presets.blurb: A rider in a tucked position, as a 2-D silhouette on a road. A stagnation region forms in front and a wide wake of shed vortices trails behind.

presets.label: Two riders
presets.name: Drafting (Two Riders)
presets.question: How does the spacing between two bodies change the wake and the drag estimate?
presets.blurb: Two rider silhouettes nose to tail. The second sits in the leader's low-speed wake, which the slipstream profile shows as a pocket where u/U drops well below one.

compare.text: Isolated rider versus two riders at the same speed; the combined wake-deficit drag is an approximation.

experiments.name: Flow around text
experiments.question: How do gaps and letter shapes redirect the flow?

presets.label: Your text
presets.name: Flow Around Your Name
presets.question: How do gaps and letter shapes redirect the flow?
presets.blurb: The pixels of a word are solid cells in the tunnel. Because obstacles are represented on the regular lattice, any shape drops in without a body-fitted mesh, and the wake braids around every letter.

experiments.name: Car silhouette
experiments.question: Where does a bluff vehicle shape shed its wake?

presets.label: Car
presets.name: Car Silhouette
presets.question: Where does a bluff vehicle shape shed its wake?
presets.blurb: A two-dimensional racing-car silhouette on a no-slip road. The flow accelerates over the body, separates at the wheels and the rear, and trails a broad unsteady wake.

experiments.name: Porous flow
experiments.question: How readily does a grain pack transmit fluid, and why?

presets.label: Default sample
presets.name: Flow Through Porous Rock
presets.question: How readily does a grain pack transmit fluid, and why?
presets.blurb: A force drives fluid through the connected gaps between solid grains. Narrow passages restrict the flow while wider channels carry more; once settled, the permeability k describes how readily the sample transmits fluid.

presets.label: Different arrangement
presets.name: Similar Porosity, Different Arrangement
presets.question: Why can equal porosity produce different permeability?
presets.blurb: The same target porosity and grain size as the default sample, but a different random arrangement. The measured porosities differ slightly (about 0.598 versus 0.600 at Medium — the random pack does not hit the target exactly; both are shown in the readouts); the paths through the pore space differ much more.

presets.label: Directional flow
presets.name: Directional Permeability
presets.question: Does the sample conduct flow equally in different directions?
presets.blurb: The same grain pack driven along y instead of x. The permeability tensor of a random pack is nearly isotropic; an arranged or elongated pack is not.

compare.text: Similar porosity, different arrangement: both measured porosities are shown; k differs by connectivity.
Same sample driven along x and along y: k_x versus k_y (force magnitude held).

experiments.name: Tracer through rock
experiments.question: How does a tracer spread as the flow carries it through a grain pack?

presets.label: Pulse, Pe 20
presets.name: Tracer Through Rock
presets.question: How does a tracer spread as the flow carries it through a grain pack?
presets.blurb: A slug of tracer is released across the inlet of the same grain pack the porous experiment uses, and the settled pore flow carries it. Wide channels run ahead, narrow ones lag and dead ends hold tracer back, so the plume spreads far faster than diffusion alone would manage and the outlet curve grows a long tail.

presets.label: Diffusion dominated, Pe 1
presets.name: Diffusion-Dominated Tracer
presets.question: What does transport look like when diffusion wins?
presets.blurb: The same sample and the same flow, but the tracer diffuses as fast as the flow carries it (Péclet number of 1). The plume stays close to symmetric, the grains only slow it down, and the outlet curve has little tail.

presets.label: Steady supply
presets.name: Advancing Tracer Front
presets.question: How sharp is the front when tracer is supplied continuously?
presets.blurb: The inlet is held at full concentration, so instead of a slug there is a front advancing through the pore space. It is never flat: it fingers along the fastest channels and lags in the tight throats, and the outlet concentration climbs towards 1.

compare.text: Diffusion dominated versus carried by the flow: the same rock and flow, Péclet number 1 against 20.
A slug against a steady supply in the same sample: breakthrough curve versus advancing front.

experiments.name: Rising smoke
experiments.question: How does buoyancy turn a smooth column into a turbulent plume?

presets.label: Smoke plume
presets.name: Rising Smoke Plume
presets.question: How does buoyancy turn a smooth column into a turbulent plume?
presets.blurb: A source of buoyant, dyed fluid at the floor. The column rises, shears against the still air, rolls up into vortices and entrains its surroundings.

experiments.name: Rayleigh–Taylor instability
experiments.question: How does the density contrast set the growth of the instability?

presets.label: Single mode
presets.name: Rayleigh–Taylor, Single Mode
presets.question: Can the early growth of one interface mode be measured consistently?
presets.blurb: A single small-amplitude cosine ripple with two wavelengths across the box. One bubble and one spike per wavelength grow before the nonlinear mushroom stage.

presets.label: Multiple modes
presets.name: Rayleigh–Taylor Fingers
presets.question: How does the density contrast set the growth of the instability?
presets.blurb: Heavy fluid rests on light fluid in gravity. The interface is unstable: spikes fall, bubbles rise, and each finger rolls up into a mushroom cap.

experiments.name: Candle flame
experiments.question: What shapes a laminar diffusion flame and makes its tip flicker?

presets.label: Flame model
presets.name: Candle Flame
presets.question: What shapes a laminar diffusion flame and makes its tip flicker?
presets.blurb: A simplified flame model: an advected mixture variable Z with a prescribed source velocity at the wick, a temperature proxy T(Z) that peaks on the stoichiometric surface, and buoyancy proportional to it. The teardrop shape and the tip flicker come from that coupling.

experiments.name: Heated-layer convection
experiments.question: When does convection develop, and how does heat transport change?

presets.label: Conduction baseline
presets.name: Heated Layer: Conduction Baseline
presets.question: What does pure conduction look like?
presets.blurb: The same layer with the buoyancy switched off. Nothing moves; heat crosses the layer by conduction only and the temperature profile stays linear.

presets.label: Convection cells
presets.name: Heated Layer: Convection Cells
presets.question: When does convection develop, and how does heat transport change?
presets.blurb: A shallow layer heated from below and cooled from above. Warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks, and the motion organises into counter-rotating cells that carry heat far faster than conduction.

presets.label: Vigorous convection
presets.name: Heated Layer: Vigorous Convection
presets.question: How does the heat transport change as the Rayleigh number grows?
presets.blurb: Stronger buoyancy and lower viscosity: the cells break into unsteady plumes and the thermal boundary layers at the plates thin.

experiments.name: Chimney plume
experiments.question: How does the plume trajectory change with wind speed?

presets.label: Calm air
presets.name: Plume in Calm Air
presets.question: What does the same source do without wind?
presets.blurb: The same stack and source with no crosswind. The plume rises vertically and meanders only through its own instability.

presets.label: Moderate crosswind
presets.name: Plume in a Crosswind
presets.question: How does the plume trajectory change with wind speed?
presets.blurb: A buoyant plume leaves a stack into a steady crosswind. Buoyancy lifts it while the wind bends it over, giving the slanted trail whose height sets how a pollutant disperses.

presets.label: Strong crosswind
presets.name: Plume in a Strong Wind
presets.question: How low does a strong wind hold the plume?
presets.blurb: The same source in the strongest recommended wind. The plume bends over close to the stack and streams downwind near the ground.

experiments.name: Sod shock tube
experiments.question: Where are the shock, the contact and the rarefaction, and how large is the error?

presets.label: Sod tube
presets.name: Sod Shock Tube
presets.question: Where are the shock, the contact and the rarefaction, and how large is the error?
presets.blurb: Two gases at different pressures separated by a membrane that bursts at t = 0. A shock runs into the low-pressure gas, a contact discontinuity follows it, and a rarefaction fan spreads the other way.

compare.text: Computed density and velocity against the exact Riemann solution, with mean absolute errors (in the diagnostics).

experiments.name: Open-air blast
experiments.question: How fast does a blast front expand, and how does it slow down?

presets.label: Blast wave
presets.name: Blast Wave in Open Air
presets.question: How fast does a blast front expand, and how does it slow down?
presets.blurb: A disc of high-pressure gas is released into still gas (a pressure-release model; no reaction or energy release is computed). It expands as a near-circular shock followed by a rarefaction that leaves a low-density core.

experiments.name: Blast and obstacles
experiments.question: How do boundaries alter shock propagation?

presets.label: Held obstacles
presets.name: Blast and Buildings (held obstacles)
presets.question: How do boundaries alter shock propagation?
presets.blurb: A ground burst beside two towers whose cells are held at a fixed dense state (an approximate reflecting obstacle, not an impermeable wall flux). The blast reflects off them, diffracts around the corners and leaves a sheltered zone in the lee of each building.

presets.label: Experimental erosion
presets.name: Blast and Buildings (erosion, experimental)
presets.question: What does a simplified erosion rule do to the towers?
presets.blurb: The same burst with an experimental rule: a solid block is removed when the overpressure on an exposed face exceeds its strength, and the gas floods the gap. Debris particles are a visual overlay, not part of the solution.

experiments.name: Shock–bubble interaction
experiments.question: How does the density contrast alter the interface deformation?

presets.label: Light bubble
presets.name: Shock Meets a Light Bubble
presets.question: How does the density contrast alter the interface deformation?
presets.blurb: A planar shock crosses a bubble of lighter gas. Misaligned pressure and density gradients deposit vorticity on the interface (the baroclinic torque) and roll the bubble into a vortex pair.

presets.label: Heavy bubble
presets.name: Shock Meets a Heavy Bubble
presets.question: What changes when the bubble is denser than the surrounding gas?
presets.blurb: The same shock hitting a bubble three times denser than the gas around it. The shock slows inside the bubble and the vorticity has the opposite sense, so the interface deforms differently.

presets.label: Twin bubbles
presets.name: Twin Bubbles
presets.question: How do two shocked interfaces interact?
presets.blurb: Two stacked light bubbles struck by the same shock. Their roll-ups interact and tangle.

experiments.name: Still-water baseline
experiments.question: Does water at rest stay at rest?

presets.label: Hydrostatic rest
presets.name: Still Water (hydrostatic baseline)
presets.question: Does water at rest stay at rest?
presets.blurb: A tank of water with nothing to disturb it. A good particle method keeps the surface flat and the velocities near zero; residual motion measures the numerical noise of the scheme.

compare.text: Residual motion and hydrostatic surface before adding waves or moving bodies.

experiments.name: Dam break
experiments.question: How does the released potential energy drive the surge?

presets.label: Dam break
presets.name: Dam Break
presets.question: How does the released potential energy drive the surge?
presets.blurb: A held-back column of water is released. Gravity converts its head into a fast surge that races along the floor, climbs the far wall and overturns.

experiments.name: Water-blob impact
experiments.question: How do impact speed and size change the splash?

presets.label: Blob impact
presets.name: Water-Blob Impact
presets.question: How do impact speed and size change the splash?
presets.blurb: A round parcel of water falls into a pool and throws up a crown-like sheet and a central jet. This is a two-dimensional blob impact without surface tension, not a resolved droplet splash.

experiments.name: Sloshing tank
experiments.question: How does the response depend on the forcing frequency?

presets.label: Sloshing
presets.name: Sloshing Tank
presets.question: How does the response depend on the forcing frequency?
presets.blurb: A tank rocked by an oscillating sideways acceleration. Near the tank's natural period the wave resonates and breaks against the walls.

experiments.name: Pouring
experiments.question: How does a continuous stream fill a container?

presets.label: Pour
presets.name: Pouring a Glass
presets.question: How does a continuous stream fill a container?
presets.blurb: Particles are emitted at a spout and fall into a tall glass, splashing as they land and settling into a rising surface.

experiments.name: Wave tank
experiments.question: What wavelength, amplitude and reflection does the wavemaker produce?

presets.label: Wave train
presets.name: Wave Tank
presets.question: What wavelength, amplitude and reflection does the wavemaker produce?
presets.blurb: A paddle (a moving wall of boundary particles) drives a train of waves along a flat-bottomed tank. They reflect from the far wall; there is no sloping beach, so no shoaling.

experiments.name: Floating hull
experiments.question: Are flotation and motion consistent with the body parameters?

presets.label: Still water
presets.name: Floating Hull: Still Water
presets.question: Are flotation and motion consistent with the body parameters?
presets.blurb: The rigid hull is placed on still water with the wavemaker stopped. It should settle to its equilibrium draught and its heave and roll should decay.

presets.label: Waves
presets.name: Floating Hull on Waves
presets.question: How does the hull respond to the wave train?
presets.blurb: The rigid hull rides the wavemaker's waves, heaving and rolling as the surface moves beneath it.

experiments.name: Kelvin–Helmholtz instability
experiments.question: How does a shear layer roll up, and how do the billows pair?

presets.label: Shear layers
presets.name: Kelvin–Helmholtz Billows
presets.question: How does a shear layer roll up, and how do the billows pair?
presets.blurb: Two layers slide past each other. The interface rolls into a row of spiral billows that pair and merge — the pattern of billow clouds and of mixing layers.

experiments.name: Decaying turbulence
experiments.question: Why do two-dimensional eddies grow as the flow decays?

presets.label: Random field
presets.name: Decaying Turbulence
presets.question: Why do two-dimensional eddies grow as the flow decays?
presets.blurb: A random swirl of vorticity left to evolve. Like-signed vortices merge into larger ones — the 2-D inverse energy cascade — while enstrophy is dissipated at small scales.

experiments.name: Taylor–Green vortex
experiments.question: Does the solver reproduce the exact viscous decay, and does it improve with refinement?

presets.label: Taylor–Green
presets.name: Taylor–Green Vortex
presets.question: Does the solver reproduce the exact viscous decay, and does it improve with refinement?
presets.blurb: A regular array of counter-rotating vortices that is an exact solution of the 2-D Navier–Stokes equations: it keeps its shape and decays as exp(−4νt).

compare.text: Computed kinetic energy against E₀·exp(−4νt) with the relative error (in the diagnostics).

experiments.name: Dye transport
experiments.question: How much apparent mixing comes from stirring and how much from diffusion?

presets.label: Diffusion only
presets.name: Dye: Diffusion Only
presets.question: How fast does diffusion alone smooth the bands?
presets.blurb: The same bands with the stirring switched off. Each band decays as a pure diffusion problem whose solution is known.

presets.label: Stirring only
presets.name: Dye: Stirring Only
presets.question: How much variance does the numerical scheme lose without physical diffusion?
presets.blurb: The same stirring with κ = 0. A conserved dye should keep its variance; the decay seen is numerical diffusion of the bilinear semi-Lagrangian advection.

presets.label: Stirring with diffusion
presets.name: Chaotic Mixing of Dye
presets.question: How much apparent mixing comes from stirring and how much from diffusion?
presets.blurb: Stripes of dye in a turbulent flow are stretched and folded into ever-finer filaments. Stirring alone cannot reduce the variance of a conserved dye; diffusion — physical and numerical — does.

compare.text: Diffusion alone versus stirring with diffusion from the same initial bands.
Stirring alone (numerical diffusion only) versus stirring with physical diffusion.

experiments.name: Gray–Scott patterns
experiments.question: Which parameter changes alter the morphology?

presets.label: Spots
presets.name: Spots
presets.question: Which parameter changes alter the morphology?
presets.blurb: Two chemicals reacting and diffusing at different rates (the Gray–Scott system) settle from noise into a field of spots. The resemblance to animal markings is suggestive; it does not establish a biological mechanism.

presets.label: Stripes/coral
presets.name: Stripes & Coral
presets.question: How does the feed/removal balance turn spots into stripes?
presets.blurb: A different (F, k) pair: spots elongate into branching stripes and coral-like ridges.

presets.label: Labyrinth
presets.name: Labyrinth
presets.question: What regime freezes into a maze?
presets.blurb: Stripes that neither close into spots nor straighten, wandering into a labyrinth.

presets.label: Replication
presets.name: Self-Replicating Spots
presets.question: Which regime makes spots divide?
presets.blurb: Blobs that grow, stretch and pinch in two — a self-replicating regime of the same equations. The name recalls cell division; the model contains no biology.

presets.label: Custom
presets.name: Gray–Scott Explorer
presets.question: Which (F, k) changes alter the morphology?
presets.blurb: Set the feed rate F and removal rate k yourself, with a reproducible seed, and map the regimes.
